flashcards.back: What can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided human reason, apart from divine revelation. The discipline this whole book belongs to.
Theology that reasons from what God is taken to have disclosed — scripture, tradition, prophecy. No premise in the five proofs comes from here.
A premise is a reason offered in support; the conclusion is what the reasons are meant to establish. Premise indicators: because, since, given that. Conclusion indicators: therefore, so, hence, thus.
An assumption an argument needs but does not state. ‘He’s a politician, so he’s lying’ hides ‘all politicians lie.’ Digging it out is usually where the real weakness turns up.
If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. A matter of form only — ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; so Fido is a reptile’ is valid.
Valid plus all premises actually true. Every sound argument is valid; not every valid argument is sound.

flashcards.front: The only two honest ways to attack a deductive argument
flashcards.back: Show that a premise is false, or show that an inference does not follow. Nothing else touches it.
Reasoning in which the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises. If the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false.
Reasoning from observed cases to a general conclusion. True premises make the conclusion probable, not guaranteed.
Accepting a hypothesis because it explains the evidence better than rivals. Probable and defeasible — and not what Feser claims to be doing.
A valid deductive argument from premises that are certain. This is the strong claim Feser makes for all five proofs.

flashcards.front: Why the demonstration claim changes how you criticize
flashcards.back: ‘Some other explanation might work’ and ‘science may yet find a cause’ are fair against best-explanation arguments and beside the point against a demonstration.
Inferring that what is true of the parts is true of the whole. ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ Not always fallacious — every brick being red does make the wall red.
Assuming in the premises the very thing to be proved. ‘The book is reliable because it says so, and what it says is true because the book is reliable.’
Refuting a weakened version of a position instead of the one actually held — e.g. attacking ‘everything has a cause, except God’, which nobody in this book holds.
Exempting a favoured case from a rule without a principled reason. Feser’s defence: the arguments supply the reason — the terminus lacks the feature that makes other things need causes.
Invoking God to fill a hole in current science, so the explanation dies when the hole closes. Feser denies his arguments have this form (ch. 7, around p. 271).
Attacking the arguer rather than the argument. ‘You only believe that because of your upbringing’ says nothing about whether the premises are true.
Exists, but could have failed to exist. You, the moon, lions. Not the everyday sense of ‘conditional on’.
Something whose existence is explained by its own nature and which could not have failed to exist. The conclusion of the rationalist proof.
A complete, non-contradictory way things could have been — not a place or a parallel universe. Limited by logic, not by physics.
A substance exists in its own right (this dog). An accident exists only in something else (the dog’s brownness). Not the everyday sense of ‘accident’ as mishap.
Matter is the stuff; form is the organizing pattern making it that kind of thing. The same bronze can have the form of a statue or of a doorstop.
Material (what it’s made of), formal (what it is), efficient (what brought it about), final (what it’s for). A chair: wood, chair-structure, carpenter, being sat on.
The way a thing really is right now. Only what is actual can do anything — potential coldness chills nothing.
A real capacity a thing has but isn’t exercising, limited by what it actually is. Coffee is potentially cold, not potentially chicken soup.
Because potentials discriminate: the coffee has some and lacks others. A concept that rules things out is not empty. This is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides.
Change would mean the new state came from nothing, which is impossible — so change is impossible. Answer: it came from a potential, which is not nothing.
The actualization of a potential. Covers qualitative (coffee cooling), local (leaf falling), quantitative (puddle growing) and substantial (fly dying) change.
Whatever actualizes a potential — including what sustains a thing in being right now, not only what got it started in the past.

flashcards.front: The two questions about a thing
flashcards.back: How did it get here? (past, historical) versus What keeps it in existence at this instant? (here-and-now). Feser almost always asks the second.
Runs back through time; members keep their power once they have it. Grandfather → father → son. Feser grants it might in principle be infinite.
Every member but the first has power only derivatively, received at the moment it acts. Cup → desk → floor → foundation → earth.
Not simultaneity — that’s just a teaching aid. It is the derivative, instrumental character of the later members.
Non-derivative — having causal power built in rather than borrowed. NOT earliest in time, NOT the Big Bang.
A brush can’t move itself, and wouldn’t if its handle were infinitely long. Length isn’t power; adding borrowers never produces a lender.

flashcards.front: Why ‘maybe the universe is infinitely old’ misses
flashcards.back: Feser explicitly grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for the sake of argument. The proof concerns hierarchical, here-and-now series.
A cause with only borrowed power, like a tool. A brush doesn’t paint — the painter paints with it. Desk, floor and foundation are instruments of the earth.
No potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it. Step 4 of chapter 1. It does NOT say ‘everything has a cause’.
Everything has an explanation of why it exists and is as it is — in something else, or in itself. Equivalently: everything is intelligible.
A cause must be distinct from its effect; a reason need not be, so something could be self-explanatory. PSR entails everything has a reason; PC does not entail everything has a cause.
Reductio: if PSR is false, we could have no reason to think we hold beliefs for good reasons — which applies to any case against PSR too. The denial is self-undermining.
A fact with no explanation at all. If the shelf stays aloft as a brute fact, it has no tendency of its own to stay up, so it can’t impart one to the book. The explanation is illusory.
Whatever is in an effect must be in its TOTAL cause somehow — formally, virtually, or eminently. A cause can’t give what it hasn’t got.
The $20: in my wallet (formally), in my bank account (virtually), or via access to a printing press (eminently).
The same feature needn’t be literally handed over — a boy needn’t have a black eye to give one. It need only be in the total cause in some way.
‘Action follows being’: a thing’s activities follow from and cannot exceed its nature. A stone cannot take in nutrients.
What a thing is — its nature, the answer to ‘what kind of thing is this?’ A human being, traditionally, is a rational animal.
The fact that a thing is, as opposed to what it is. You can grasp what a unicorn is and know that there are none.

flashcards.front: Real distinction vs. distinction of reason
flashcards.back: A real distinction tracks mind-independent reality; a distinction of reason is only in our thinking — ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ pick out the same thing.

flashcards.front: Argument from knowledge for the real distinction
flashcards.back: Describe lions, pterodactyls and unicorns fully to someone unfamiliar with all three; he still can’t say which exists. So essence doesn’t deliver existence.

flashcards.front: Argument from contingency for the real distinction
flashcards.back: If a lion’s existence were part of its essence, it would exist by its very nature and couldn’t fail to exist. Lions are contingent, so the distinction is real.

flashcards.front: Argument from uniqueness for the real distinction
flashcards.back: There could be at most one thing whose essence just is existence — differentiating two would make each ‘existence itself PLUS something’. Ordinary kinds come in multiples.
That whose essence just is existence — the conclusion of the Thomistic proof. Latin: ipsum esse subsistens. It can impart existence without receiving it.
A general pattern many particular things exhibit — redness, triangularity, humanness. The pattern, not the collection of instances.
Real, but not in space or time, and not causally interacting: universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds. Not ‘vague’ or ‘imaginary’.
‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ are two sentences expressing one proposition. Erase both and the proposition is still true.
Realism: universals are real independently of us. Nominalism: only particulars exist; universals are just names. Conceptualism: universals are concepts in human minds.

flashcards.front: Why ch. 3 rejects nominalism and conceptualism
flashcards.back: Both make abstract truths depend on us. But seven was prime before humans existed and would be if humanity vanished. Names and concepts are things we make.
Universals are mind-independent with respect to OUR minds, but exist as ideas in a divine intellect — not in a Platonic third realm.
Made of parts — physical or metaphysical. A composite depends at every moment on its parts existing and being united.
Really distinct principles within one thing, not separable objects: form/matter, essence/existence, substance/accidents, act/potency, genus/difference.

flashcards.front: Why a composite can’t unite its own parts
flashcards.back: It exists only given that union, so explaining the union by it would be an explanatory circle. Something distinct from it must account for the union.
Having NO parts of any kind. Not ‘easy to understand’ — Feser holds God to be incomprehensible, and simplicity is a large part of why.
God as pure actuality: simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good — the source of existence, not a being among beings.
God as the unique member of a species under the genus person — immensely powerful, but composite. The recent departure, not the tradition.
…whether God is personal. Most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God. The dispute is whether God falls under a genus and is composite.
No unrealized potentials whatever. The conclusion of the Aristotelian proof, and the root from which nearly every other divine attribute is derived.

flashcards.front: How the divine attributes are derived
flashcards.back: One repeating pattern: attribute X would require an unactualized potential; pure actuality has none; therefore not-X. Steps 19–32 of chapter 1.
Outside time altogether, not endless duration. Existing in time would involve change, which pure actuality excludes.
Being that from which ALL causal power derives — not ‘can do anything describable, including contradictions’.
The world could not exist even for an instant unless God were continually sustaining it in being. The opposite of deism.
The rival thesis that once a thing exists it simply continues on its own, needing no sustaining cause. Named by analogy with Newtonian inertia.
Univocal: same sense (‘Fido is a dog’ / ‘Rover is a dog’). Equivocal: unrelated (bat in the attic / bat in your hand). Analogical: related but not identical (‘good wine’ / ‘good man’).
‘God is good’ is a literal claim used analogically. ‘God is a rock’ is metaphor. Feser objects to calling Aquinas’ view ‘analogical rather than literal’.
Many attacks on divine simplicity assume univocity — e.g. ‘power and knowledge are distinct in us, so must be in God.’ Analogy blocks the inference.
No argument uses ‘everything has a cause’. And each explains why its terminus couldn’t have a cause: it has no potentials, no parts, no essence distinct from existence, no contingency.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘why can’t the regress be infinite?’
flashcards.back: For linear series, Feser agrees it might be. For hierarchical series, every member is a borrower, and no number of borrowers produces a lender.
Zeus is a powerful being inside the universe; classical theism’s God is the source of existence itself. Rejecting the first doesn’t commit you to rejecting the second (ch. 7, pp. 289–292).
Science asks how things within the world behave; these arguments ask why anything exists and what sustains it. A finished physics wouldn’t touch the question.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘isn’t this just faith dressed up?’
flashcards.back: That’s an ad hominem about arguers, not arguments. Natural theology uses no premise from revelation, and the arguments tell you exactly how to refute them.
Demonstrations are refuted by false premises or invalid steps, not by head-counts. Feser addresses whether a proof can be controversial at the end of ch. 7 (p. 307).
Imaginability isn’t the test of intelligibility. You can’t picture the number seventeen or a thousand-sided polygon, yet you reason about both rigorously.
1. Informal Stage 1 (something fitting a description exists). 2. Informal Stage 2 (it must have the divine attributes). 3. Formal numbered statement. 4. Objections.
Answering ‘even if there’s a first cause, why call it God?’ — the objection you’ll meet most often. Skipping Stage 2 leaves you unable to answer it.
It’s a recap, not new material. Break into blocks (1–5 setup, 6–14 to pure actuality, 15–18 uniqueness, 19–47 attributes). Label each step. Ask which one you’d challenge.
These are inferences. They need only a valid link to earlier steps — the independent defence belongs to the premises, which is where you should spend your attention.

flashcards.front: The five thinkers and their questions
flashcards.back: Aristotle: how is change possible? Plotinus: what holds parts together? Augustine: where do the patterns live? Aquinas: why does anything exist? Leibniz: why anything rather than nothing?

flashcards.front: What Feser says his book is NOT
flashcards.back: Not a book about Aquinas’ Five Ways, not textual exegesis of anyone, and not preceded by a long metaphysical prolegomenon — the background is introduced as needed.
The claim that science is the only source of knowledge. Self-defeating, since the claim itself isn’t a scientific result. Chapter 7 develops this from around p. 273.
Leibniz: each copy is explained by the previous copy, infinitely. Yet why the series contains geometry at all is untouched. Used against the fallacy-of-composition charge.

For each chapter keep: TERMS (word, definition, page) / STEPS (the argument in your words) / OBJECTIONS (objection, reply, how convinced 1–5) / QUESTIONS (what you didn’t follow, with pages).
